world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: vinc1243 is not in the catalog. Two title hits: (1) Hill 2019 (Folia Linguistica Historica) is a false hit — Glottolog's record says the Vincentian tag is a 'computerized assignment from \"apparent\"'; the abstract (Crossref/S2) is about the Prosodic Change Hypothesis in historical sound change, nothing on Vincentian; closed access, priority none. (2) Prescod 2006 (STUF 59(2):191-210) was obtained and read in the author's own open French translation on HAL (hal-01115827; HAL's Anubis bot-wall meant the file was pulled from the Internet Archive copy. It is mostly post-lexical (intensity/F0 disambiguation of 8 utterance pairs in Praat); at word level it says only that lexical stress distinguishes N/V pairs as in English, that inter-syllable intensity differences are very small, and that the pitch-contrasted pair bròdà/brôdà both bear initial stress — no general placement rule. The English original (paywalled De Gruyter) remains unread, priority medium. Best first-hand statement found: Prescod's APiCS survey chapter (2013, §4 Phonology): 'In polysyllabic words, stress is generally assigned to the first syllable.., failing which, stress falls on the syllable that contains a long vowel or a diphthong.. and on the syllable before -shan and -zan' — initial default with weight- and suffix-driven overrides; this would be the deciding source if a catalog record is created.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable of a polysyllabic word; a syllable containing a long vowel or diphthong attracts the stress instead (teliˈfoon); words in the suffixes -shan/-zan (< English -tion/-sion) stress the syllable before the suffix (badaˈreishan, teliˈvizan). Prescod 2006 adds that a demarcative lexical accent distinguishes noun from verb (taamentN/taamentV), so some contrasts are lexical, as in the English lexifier.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Long-vowel/diphthong syllables and the -shan/-zan suffix rule are the stated departures from initial stress; Prescod 2006 (p. 2) notes N/V pairs distinguished by stress placement and (pp. 4-5) that at the lexical level intensity differences between syllables are very small, with duration and pitch doing most of the work.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (polysyllabic lexical words); Prescod 2006 treats phrase-level (post-lexical, pragmatic) accent and pitch separately and finds high pitch marks pragmatic accent in utterances.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for Vincentian Creole proper (mainland St Vincent, autoglossonym Vincy), glottocode vinc1243, described by its principal researcher Paula Prescod. The Bequia (Grenadines) variety studied by Meyerhoff & Walker and Daleszynska has no separate glottocode and no stress statement was found for it.

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the language's principal describer (native speaker, author of the only instrumental prosody study). Default word stress is initial in polysyllables; this default is overridden by syllable weight (a long vowel or diphthong attracts stress, e.g. teliˈfoon) and by the suffixes -shan/-zan, which place stress on the immediately pre-suffixal syllable (badaˈreishan, teliˈvizan). So: weight-sensitive, morphologically conditioned stress with an initial default — not a fixed-position system; noun/verb pairs can also be stress-distinguished (Prescod 2006, p. 2 of the HAL version), and pitch contour rather than intensity separates some polysyllabic lexical pairs (bròdà/brôdà).

sources.quote: « Comme en anglais, non seulement peut-on employer l'accent lexical démarcatif pour différencier un item nominal d'un item verbal tel que dans taamentN et taamentV » (p. 2) … « Nos mesures acoustiques affirment qu'en VinC, il y a très peu de différence d'intensité entre les syllabes au niveau lexical. […] dans des paires polysyllabiques, ni la durée ni l'intensité ne semblent avoir d'effet sur l'interprétation sémantique. […] les deux mots portent l'accent tonique sur la première syllabe » (p. 4; bròdà 'frère (famille)' vs brôdà 'frère (ordre religieux)')
sources.locator: HAL French version p. 2 (§1 Introduction) and p. 4 (§2.2 'Le rôle des suprasegmentaux dans l'identification des paires minimales'); ≈ STUF pp. 192-195 of the English original
sources.note: Instrumental (Praat) study of 8 segmentally identical utterance pairs; does not give a general word-stress rule. States (p. 2) that, as in English, a demarcative lexical accent distinguishes noun from verb (taamentN / taamentV 'torment'); (p. 4, ex. 7) in the disyllabic pair bròdà 'brother (kin)' / brôdà 'brother (religious)' 'les deux mots portent l'accent tonique sur la première syllabe', and lexical-level intensity differences between syllables are very small, so duration (vowel length) and pitch do the disambiguating; the rest of the paper is about post-lexical/pragmatic accent and pitch…
